{ "item": { "id": "3dee93e3-891a-46f3-a05a-9c4e6927c709", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Error handling & recovery", "short_description": "How Godzilla retries failed events, when they're dead-lettered, and how to replay them.", "body": "

Error handling & recovery

Every event that fails a transform or a destination write is retried automatically. This guide covers how that works and what to do when retries run out.

Automatic retries

Failed events retry with exponential backoff — 1s, 2s, 4s, up to a per-pipeline configurable ceiling. Most transient failures (a destination hiccup, a rate-limited third party) resolve within the first few attempts.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=pipeline-retry-config.json|language=json|code={ "retry_policy": { "max_attempts": 5, "backoff": "exponential", "initial_delay_ms": 1000 } }}}

Dead-lettering

An event that exhausts its retries is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped silently.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=danger|title=Dead-lettered events don't retry themselves|body_html=

Once in the dead-letter queue, an event stays there until you replay it or explicitly discard it — it will not retry again on its own.

}}

Replaying events

Use the Events endpoint's replay action to re-run a specific dead-lettered event once the underlying issue is fixed.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=replay.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/events/evt_8f2c1a90/replay \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY"}}

Watching for failures

Subscribe to pipeline.failed via Webhooks so you find out about dead-lettered events before a customer does. See also Monitoring & alerts.

{ "item": { "id": "086daf0b-cd40-46ec-8246-c67e0a8530a4", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Scheduling & triggers", "short_description": "Run a pipeline on a cron schedule or trigger it directly from incoming events.", "body": "

Scheduling & triggers

A pipeline runs either on a schedule or in response to incoming events. This guide covers both.

Scheduled pipelines

Set a schedule (a cron expression) when creating or updating a pipeline via the Pipelines endpoint. Godzilla runs the pipeline once per schedule tick, processing whatever new data is available from the source since the last run.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=schedule.json|language=json|code={ "schedule": "0 */4 * * *" }}}

Event-triggered pipelines

Omit schedule and the pipeline instead runs continuously, processing events as its source connector emits them — the right choice for sources like Kafka or a Webhook connector where near-real-time matters.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Choosing between them|body_html=

Use a schedule for sources that batch naturally (a nightly file drop to S3). Use event-triggered for anything where minutes matter.

}}

Pausing and resuming

A paused pipeline skips scheduled ticks entirely and buffers nothing for event-triggered sources — resuming picks up new events going forward, not a backlog. To reprocess a time range instead, see the replay flow in Error handling & recovery.

{{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|prev_label=Error handling & recovery|next_href={{cms:item/522ba05b-8a21-43dd-82ac-ece908ce14b4}}|next_label=Monitoring & alerts}}", "version_token": "2e915fe4-5f8a-4c91-b032-9b1c840d427e", "created_at": "2026-08-21T12:42:14.267Z", "updated_at": "2026-08-21T12:42:19.670Z", "placement_id": "8ed279da-c9eb-46e0-bd2f-4f15df9f1c76", "folder_id": "c3e0ba4a-a491-4265-9848-556d298e6b6b", "file_name": "scheduling-and-triggers" } }

Connecting a data source

This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

Choosing a connector type

You haveUse
A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
Files landing in object storageAmazon S3

Authenticating

Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

}}

Verifying the connection

A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

Transforming events in flight

As events flow through your Godzilla pipeline, you often need to modify them to match downstream system requirements, remove sensitive data, or add context. This guide walks you through the transformation patterns available in Godzilla.

Overview

Event transformation happens at three key points in a pipeline:

  • At the source: Select and map fields from the incoming event
  • In transit: Apply filters, enrichments, and reshaping logic
  • At the destination: Format the event for the target system

Reshaping events

Reshaping allows you to restructure event payloads—flattening nested objects, combining fields, or splitting a single event into multiple events. Use the transformation builder to:

  • Map source fields to new names and paths
  • Create new calculated fields from existing data
  • Flatten or nest objects as needed

Filtering events

Filters determine which events proceed through the pipeline and which are dropped. Apply conditions based on:

  • Event field values (e.g., only process orders over $100)
  • Event age or timing
  • Presence or absence of required fields

Filtered-out events are tracked in your pipeline metrics so you can monitor whether your filter rules are working as expected.

Enriching events

Enrichment adds context to events using external data sources or internal lookups. Common enrichment patterns include:

  • Looking up customer details from a database or API
  • Adding geolocation data from IP addresses
  • Appending feature flags or A/B test assignments

Enrichment happens synchronously—the pipeline waits for the lookup to complete before forwarding the event.

Chaining transformations

Transformations can be stacked to apply multiple operations to a single event. The order matters: filters typically come first (to avoid processing events you don't need), followed by reshaping, then enrichment.

Monitoring transformed events

After applying transformations, use the pipeline inspector to:

  • Preview the shape of transformed events before publishing
  • Check filter pass/fail rates in real time
  • Track enrichment latency and failure counts

Building your first pipeline

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Create a source connector
  • Create a destination connector
  • Create the pipeline
  • Next steps
    • }}

    This guide walks through creating a pipeline end to end: a source connector, a destination connector, and the pipeline that ties them together.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Before you start|body_html=

    You'll need an API key. See Authentication in Getting Started if you don't have one yet.

    }}

    1. Create a source connector

    We'll pull orders from Postgres. See Connectors for the full catalog of types.

    Using curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-source.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"type":"postgres","direction":"source","config":{"connection_string":"postgres://..."}}'}}

    Using Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"fmt"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-sh/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\\t\\tos.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"),\\n\\t)\\n\\n\\tconnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\\t\\tType: "postgres",\\n\\t\\tDirection: "source",\\n\\t\\tConfig: map[string]interface(){\\n\\t\\t\\t"connection_string": "postgres://...",\\n\\t\\t},\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tfmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error: %v\\n", err)\\n\\t\\tos.Exit(1)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tfmt.Printf("Created source connector: %s\\n", connector.ID)\\n}}}

    2. Create a destination connector

    We'll write to Snowflake.

    Using curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-destination.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/connectors \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"type":"snowflake","direction":"destination","config":{"account":"..."}}'}}

    Using Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"fmt"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-sh/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\\t\\tos.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"),\\n\\t)\\n\\n\\tconnector, err := client.Connectors.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreateConnectorRequest{\\n\\t\\tType: "snowflake",\\n\\t\\tDirection: "destination",\\n\\t\\tConfig: map[string]interface(){\\n\\t\\t\\t"account": "...",\\n\\t\\t},\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tfmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error: %v\\n", err)\\n\\t\\tos.Exit(1)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tfmt.Printf("Created destination connector: %s\\n", connector.ID)\\n}}}

    3. Create the pipeline

    Full request/response details are in the Pipelines endpoint reference.

    Using curl

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=create-pipeline.sh|language=bash|code=curl -X POST https://api.godzilladocs.dev/v2/pipelines \\\\\\n -H "Authorization: Bearer $GODZILLA_API_KEY" \\\\\\n -d '{"name":"ingest-orders","source_connector_id":"conn_pg_orders","destination_connector_id":"conn_snowflake_dw"}'}}

    Using Go

    {{ds:component/code-block|filename=main.go|language=go|code=package main\\n\\nimport (\\n\\t"context"\\n\\t"fmt"\\n\\t"os"\\n\\n\\t"github.com/godzilla-sh/godzilla-go"\\n)\\n\\nfunc main() {\\n\\tclient := godzilla.NewClient(\\n\\t\\tos.Getenv("GODZILLA_API_KEY"),\\n\\t)\\n\\n\\tpipeline, err := client.Pipelines.Create(context.Background(), &godzilla.CreatePipelineRequest{\\n\\t\\tName: "ingest-orders",\\n\\t\\tSourceConnectorID: "conn_pg_orders",\\n\\t\\tDestinationConnectorID: "conn_snowflake_dw",\\n\\t})\\n\\tif err != nil {\\n\\t\\tfmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "Error: %v\\n", err)\\n\\t\\tos.Exit(1)\\n\\t}\\n\\n\\tfmt.Printf("Created pipeline: %s (state: %s)\\n", pipeline.ID, pipeline.State)\\n}}}

    The pipeline starts in draft state. Activate it once you're ready to start processing events.

    Next steps

    Now that events are flowing, read Handling errors & retries to see what happens when a write fails, or Monitoring & alerts to watch it run.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/60d7d27a-ceda-4034-b98e-8b1181ca5c84}}|prev_label=Guides|next_href={{cms:item/3448ffab-598c-46e7-bda6-e7cdc4a1e7c6}}|next_label=Connecting a data source}}

Connecting a data source

{{ds:component/docs-toc|items_html=
  • Choosing a connector type
  • Authenticating
  • Verifying the connection
  • Next steps
    • }}

    This guide covers choosing and configuring a source connector — the first step of any new pipeline.

    Choosing a connector type

    You haveUse
    A relational database you can grant replication access toPostgres
    Files landing in object storageAmazon S3
    An existing event streamKafka
    A third party that can push to a URL you controlWebhook

    Authenticating

    Each connector type has its own credential shape — see the Connectors endpoint for the full parameter list per type.

    {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Least-privilege credentials|body_html=

    Grant the connector only the access it needs — read-only replication for Postgres sources, a scoped IAM role for S3, never a superuser or admin credential.

    }}

    Verifying the connection

    A newly created connector reports health: degraded until its first successful read or write, then flips to healthy. If it goes straight to down, double check credentials before opening a support ticket.

    Next steps

    With a source connected, follow Building your first pipeline to wire it into a full pipeline.

    {{ds:component/docs-pagination|prev_href={{cms:item/2df76640-838b-4256-956e-d8a19a602241}}|prev_label=Building your first pipeline|next_href={{cms:item/062cc815-2b65-45b1-b36c-6ea67dfd1a0c}}|next_label=Error handling & recovery}}
